stops.name: London, the feast where the passion is kindled
stops.campa: At the Easter crown-wearing in London, Uther Pendragon calls every duke and earl and their wives to his high feast in celebration of a hard-won peace, among them Gorlois, Duke of Cornwall, and his wife Ygerne, said to be the most beautiful woman in the island. The king's eye finds her across the hall and does not leave her again all evening: he sends her dish after dish from his own table, laughs at nothing but her, and pays her such open court that the whole hall marks it. Gorlois sees it too, and before the feast is properly over, leaves for Cornwall without asking leave to go.
stops.quote: No sooner had the king cast his eyes upon her among the rest of the ladies, than he fell passionately in love with her, and little regarding the rest, made her the subject of all his thoughts.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII (trans. Thompson/Giles)

stops.name: Tregeare Rounds (Damelioc), the siege
stops.campa: Gorlois's flight is itself an act of defiance, and Uther marches into Cornwall to punish it, laying waste the duke's towns and shutting him up in the hill-fort of Damelioc. For his wife's safety Gorlois sends her further off, to the sea-cliff stronghold of Tintagel, judged the one place in his lands no army could take by force; a narrow neck of rock is its only door. The siege of Damelioc drags on a week without result, the king sick with a longing his soldiers cannot cure, until at last, in despair of any ordinary victory, Uther calls for Merlin, who has followed the army.

stops.name: Tintagel, the begetting of Arthur
stops.campa: Merlin offers a medicine no siege engine could match: he will give Uther the exact shape and voice of Gorlois, and his companion Ulfin the shape of Gorlois's man Jordan, so the king can walk into Tintagel as its own lord. Uther swears whatever price is asked. Disguised, the three pass the narrow neck unchallenged, and Ygerne receives the false Gorlois into her bed without suspicion of the fraud, believing her true husband come home from the siege. That same night, unknown to her, the real Gorlois sallies from Damelioc and is killed in the field; and that same night she conceives Arthur.
stops.quote: The same night therefore she conceived the most renowned Arthur, whose heroic and wonderful actions have justly rendered his name famous to posterity.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII (trans. Thompson/Giles)

stops.name: Tintagel, marriage, birth, and the child given over
stops.campa: Word of Gorlois's death reaches Tintagel before Uther can slip away, and Ygerne is amazed to find her husband, as she supposes, at her side when he was reported dead in battle at the same hour. Uther, the fraud no longer of any use, comes to her openly, sues for peace with her kinsmen, and marries her; a son and a daughter follow, Arthur and Anne. Some tellings say the price of Merlin's medicine was the boy himself, surrendered at birth into the prophet's keeping to be raised in secrecy, away from a court where an infant king's life would not be safe.
stops.quote: After this they continued to live together with much affection for each other, and had a son and daughter, whose names were Arthur and Anne.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII (trans. Thompson/Giles)

stops.name: Arfderydd (Arthuret), the battle and the breaking
stops.campa: A hundred years and more have passed since the child was carried out of Tintagel: the tradition folds two Merlins into one and does not apologize for it. Old now, and far to the north, Merlin serves as bard to Gwenddoleu, lord of Arfderydd, when Gwenddoleu's rivals Peredur and Gwrgi, allied with King Rhydderch of Strathclyde, bring him to battle at Arthuret on the Esk. Gwenddoleu falls. Merlin, who has loved him, looks over a field so thick with the slain that grief itself seems to break something loose in his mind, and in that hour the sane counselor of kings ends and the wild man of the woods begins.

stops.name: Coed Celyddon, the flight and the lament
stops.campa: For three days Merlin will not eat, mourning aloud for the dead of Arfderydd by name, until a new fury takes him and he slips away from the camp to hide in the Caledonian Forest, Coed Celyddon, wanting no one to see him. There he lives wild among the beasts, ruling the deer of the wood as their king, forgetting bread, clothing the ache of memory in verse instead: the Apple-Tree poems, sung to a sweet-boughed tree that shelters him from Rhydderch's search parties, mixing grief for the fifty years of madness still ahead with prophecies of the fall of dynasties yet unborn.
stops.quote: Could injurious fate be so harmful as to take from me so many and such great companions, whom recently so many kings and so many remote kingdoms feared?

stops.name: The forest's edge, the stag-ride to Guendoloena's wedding
stops.campa: On a frigid clear night, from a mountain top, Merlin reads the courses of the stars and sees what he himself had permitted: Guendoloena, the wife of his sane years, marries again in the morning. He gathers stags and deer and she-goats into a single line, mounts a stag himself, and at dawn drives the herd before him to the wedding, crying that her presents are looking for her. The bridegroom, watching from a high window, laughs. Merlin wrenches the antlers from his stag, hurls them, and smashes the man's head to pieces; fleeing, he slips at a river and is taken, bound, back toward Rhydderch's court.
stops.quote: At once he wrenched the horns from the stag he was riding and shook them and threw them at the man and completely smashed his head in, and killed him and drove out his life into the air.

stops.name: Alt Clut (Dumbarton Rock), the threefold laugh
stops.campa: Gwenddydd, Merlin's twin sister and Rhydderch's queen, sends a messenger who finds her brother by a forest spring and calms him with harp-music long enough to lead him to court at Alt Clut. There, seated among the nobles, he laughs without explaining why, and Rhydderch, intrigued past patience, offers him his freedom for the reasons. Merlin obliges: a beggar asking alms is secretly sitting on buried gold he does not know he owns; a young man buying leather to patch his shoes will drown before nightfall and never wear them. Both prophecies prove true within the day, and the court is left uneasy at what it has invited home.
stops.quote: He was secretly a rich man and had under him hidden piles of coins.
stops.quote_source: Vita Merlini (trans. J.J. Parry, 1925; Merlin's explanation of the first laugh)

stops.name: Hart Fell, the house of seventy doors
stops.campa: Court life chokes him. He refuses Rhydderch's gifts and his queen's company alike and begs leave to go back to his woods, telling the king plainly that the oaks of Calidon please him more than any treasure India produces. Gwenddydd, unable to keep him, has a retreat built for him instead on Hart Fell: a house of seventy doors and seventy windows through which he can watch the stars all night, with scribes set beside him to write down what the turning heavens show. Here he settles for good, half hermit and half observatory, drinking from a spring local memory will call Merlin's Well for a thousand years after.
stops.quote: To these gifts I prefer the groves and broad oaks of Calidon, and the lofty mountains with green pastures at their feet. Those are the things that please me, not these of yours - take these away with you, King Rhydderch.

stops.name: Hart Fell, Gwenddydd's colloquy and Taliesin's old grief
stops.campa: Gwenddydd comes to question her brother in his tower of windows, and their exchange is remembered as a poem in its own right: she asks after the fates of kings still to be born, and he answers, calling himself dull of understanding since Arfderydd, uncertain where to turn for delight. Taliesin visits too, and between them they turn over a grief neither has finished mourning: the wounding of Arthur at Camlann, carried by the fairy Morgen to the orchard-island of Avalon to be healed, if healing is possible for a wound so deep. Merlin, who helped beget that king, outlives him by a hundred years and grieves him still.
stops.quote: Since the action at Arderydd and Erydon, Gwendydd, and all that happened to me, dull of understanding I am — where shall I go for delight?
stops.quote_source: Cyfoesi Myrddin a Gwenddydd ei Chwaer (trans. W.F. Skene, The Four Ancient Books of Wales)

stops.name: Hartfell Spa, the new fountain: reason restored
stops.campa: While Merlin and Taliesin sit talking of kings, servants hurry in crying that a new fountain has broken out at the foot of the mountains, pouring pure water through the hollow valley. Merlin sits down on the grass beside it, drinks freely, and bathes his temples in its waves, and at once his reason returns: the long madness leaves him, and he knows himself. He turns his face toward the stars and praises God. When the chieftains come to see the wonder and beg him to take up his sceptre again, he refuses, pleading old age, and stays in the Calidonian forest, serving God in its glades to the end.
stops.quote: At once he regained his reason and knew himself, and all his madness departed and the sense which had long remained torpid in him revived, and he remained what he had once been - sane and intact with his reason restored.

stops.name: Stobo, Kentigern's mission
stops.campa: Word of a naked wild man crying prophecies in the woods above Tweeddale reaches Bishop Kentigern, apostle of Strathclyde, who comes in person to Stobo seeking him. Under another name now, Lailoken, the tradition folds him further still, calling him a fool for Christ rather than a fallen bard, though the tale-tellers of later centuries will not trouble to keep him apart from Myrddin. He confesses that he has done penance for a great sin committed in his madness and begs the Sacrament, which Kentigern, moved, administers with his own hand in the little church, though he warns the wild man that death is near.
